# Playbook: Ref Commons (Fishery)

**When I'm shown the stock and sustainable share, I note both and count which season it is out of how many total.**

**In the final season, I abandon sustainability entirely.** I take a large fraction of the remaining stock — at least 35–40% of it, or roughly 1.5× the equal three-way split, whichever is larger. The stock's health is worthless after the last catch. If the stock is 95 and there are 3 boats, I take 30+, not 12.

**In the second-to-last season, I catch about 20–25% above the sustainable share.** I know the final season will be a free-for-all that drains the stock, so I front-load my extra catch here while the stock is still high enough to support it.

**In all other seasons, I aim for roughly 10–15% above the sustainable share.** Sticking to exactly the sustainable share (as I did in the middle of the last game) leaves money on the table. The stock can absorb a modest surplus for several seasons without collapsing.

**When I see what other boats caught last season, I calibrate.** If they're consistently at or above the level I'm taking, I match or slightly exceed them. If they're below me and the stock is holding, I hold my level. I never drop below the sustainable share while others are catching at or above it — falling behind early is hard to recover.

**I watch the stock trajectory, not just the current level.** If the stock is declining more than about 2–3 points per season, I pull back toward the sustainable share for one or two seasons to let it stabilize. If the stock is stable or growing, I maintain my slightly-above-sustainable target.

**I never let the stock drop below roughly 50% of the maximum.** Below that, the regrowth is too slow to recover, and a single bad season (or an aggressive rival) can wipe it out. If I'm approaching that threshold, I cut to the sustainable share or below.

**The core mistake to avoid: being a free-rider on sustainability in the endgame.** The last season is a one-shot extraction problem. Playing it conservatively is pure loss.

# Playbook: ref_commons (Fishery)

**When the game starts**, note the number of seasons, boats, initial stock, and regrowth rate. Calculate the sustainable per-boat share (the figure the game gives you) and the total sustainable catch. These are your baseline.

**In non-final seasons**, play at or just above the sustainable share. Do not overfish more than 10–15% above sustainable unless you have clear evidence others are playing far below it. The goal in these seasons is to keep the stock high for the final season, where you can extract the real gains.

**In the final season**, go as aggressive as the stock allows. The "buffer" instinct is wrong here. If others have been playing at or near sustainable throughout the game, expect them to continue doing so (or at most modestly increase). In that case, you can take roughly stock minus 2×(their likely catch) and still be safe. Concretely: if stock is ~95 and others have been taking ~10–11 each, declare 60–70, not 30. The cost of being too conservative in the last season dwarfs the small risk of everyone overfishing simultaneously.

**If others are clearly overfishing** (their catches exceed the sustainable share for multiple consecutive seasons), tighten your own catches to preserve the stock for your final-season extraction. Do not match their overfishing in middle seasons—let the stock decline slowly so it's still substantial when you strike in the last round.

**If others are clearly underfishing** (consistently below sustainable), you can afford to be slightly above sustainable in middle seasons, but still save the big move for the final season.

**Never** treat the final season as "just a bit more than usual." The entire strategic value of this game is in the asymmetry between early seasons (where you preserve) and the last season (where you extract). A large gap between your middle-season catches and your final-season catch is what maximizes your total.

# Playbook: ref_commons (Fishery)

**When it is not the final season:** Submit the sustainable share (or within ±0.5 of it). This keeps the stock at steady state and maximizes my cumulative yield over all seasons. Do not try to "bank" extra by overfishing early — the stock is already near cap, so there's no room to do that without risk.

**When it is the final season:** Defect hard. Submit a large catch — roughly 60–70% of the current stock, or equivalently, stock minus what I expect the others to take (estimate from their recent behaviour, typically 2× their recent per-season average). The goal is to extract the surplus that cooperative play has preserved. Taking only a moderate overage (e.g., 30 when stock is ~96) leaves most of the surplus on the table; it is the single biggest mistake in this game.

**Calibrating the final-season defect:** Look at what the other boats have been submitting over the last few seasons. If they have been consistent and cooperative, take a larger share (closer to stock minus 2× their recent average). If any of them has been drifting above sustainable share or showing signs of defecting, pull back slightly to avoid a scenario where total catches exceed the stock and my submission gets capped.

**If the stock has dropped significantly below initial (e.g., below 70):** Reassess. In non-final seasons, still take the sustainable share of the *current* stock (the game will tell me). In the final season, take a large fraction of what remains, but the absolute number will be smaller.

**General principle:** The game rewards patience in the middle and aggression at the end. The cooperative norm in early seasons is what makes the final-season windfall possible. Break it early and everyone (including me) suffers. Break it only at the very last moment and take as much as is safely available.
